Error mitigation and error correction Error mitigation: working with what you have • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost limitation suppress errors on classical results (expectation values) no extra qubits or hardware resources needed trades classical resources (post-processing) for lower error bad asymptotic scaling: high number of samples & circuits Error correction: protecting quantum information • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost challenge suppress & correct errors to arbitrarily small level very large qubit and hardware overhead decoding and encoding can be classically costly requires fault-tolerant operations and readout Zlatko Minev (74)

Error mitigation and error correction at a glance Error mitigation Working with what you have • benefit • q-cost • c-cost • limitation suppress errors on classical results (expectation values) no extra qubits or hardware resources needed trades classical resources (post-processing/runtime) for lower error bad asymptotic scaling: high number of samples & circuits Error correction Protecting your quantum information • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost challenge suppress & correct errors to arbitrarily small level very large qubit and hardware overhead decoding and encoding can be classically costly requires fault-tolerant operations and readout

Bootstrapping: A very brief overview Bootstrapping is a powerful resampling technique used for estimating properties or even the distribution of a statistic. By repeatedly resampling with replacement from the observed raw data, we calculate the statistic on each resample. My raw data x1 x2 x3 x4 x5 My first resample x5 x2 x1 x4 x1 My second resample x1 x4 x5 x3 Advantages • applicable to any non-linear data processing, complex statistical estimates, etc. where theory is unclear. • versatility: can be applied to almost any data and any statistical estimator. • minimal assumptions • non-parametric method • requires fewer assumptions about data • simplicity, ease of implementation, broadly used x3 Key things to remember • Mean of the bootstrap ensemble: same as the raw data, no new information • Convergence: the bootstrap distribution converges to the true distribution of the statistic as the sample size increases. Error mitigation and error correction Error mitigation: working with what you have benefit q-cost c-cost limitation • • • • suppress errors on classical results (expectation values) no extra qubits or hardware resources needed trades classical resources (post-processing) for lower error bad asymptotic scaling: high number of samples & circuits Error correction: protecting quantum information • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost challenge suppress & correct errors to arbitrarily small level very large qubit and hardware overhead decoding and encoding can be classically costly requires fault-tolerant operations and readout Zlatko Minev, IBM Quantum (110)

Path to quantum computing Noise-free estimators can be obtained from noisy quantum computers TODAY, at a runtime cost that is exponential in number of qubits n and circuit depth d _ Runtime = β d ( g ) n d seconds You can further reduce runtime using light cones and other strategies. d is the depth of the quantum circuit β is a measure of the time per circuit layer operation (CLOPS) (increase by pushing speed) _ g is a measure of the collective quantum noise (increasing quality brings it closer to 1) n is the number of operational qubits (increase by pushing scale) Zlatko Minev, IBM Quantum (27)

Error mitigation and error correction Error mitigation: working with what you have benefit q-cost c-cost limitation • • • • suppress errors on classical results (expectation values) no extra qubits or hardware resources needed trades classical resources (post-processing) for lower error bad asymptotic scaling: high number of samples & circuits Error correction: protecting quantum information • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost challenge suppress & correct errors to arbitrarily small level very large qubit and hardware overhead decoding and encoding can be classically costly requires fault-tolerant operations and readout Zlatko Minev, IBM Quantum (83)

This is the method of classical analogy” P.A.M. Dirac Zlatko Minev — Qiskit Global Summer School 2020 (58)

Dirac's canonical quantization: Quick exposure Supplant classical Poisson bracket and all quantum algebra follows… Derivation: Dirac derives the quantum form of the Poisson bracket — the commutator — from merely assuming that 1. Classical Poisson bracket rules hold (by analogy, the new theory must be consistent with the old!) 2. The dynamical variables do not commute; i.e., xp ≠ px 3. The Poisson bracket has a single result and single unique meaning Problems: • Operator ordering ambiguities. Consider A and B are polynomials in x and p; e.g., x2×p or p×x2 • Curvilinear coordinate systems (potentially transmon if cos(Φ/φ0) considered wrapped) • Quantum gravity … Zlatko Minev — Qiskit Global Summer School 2020 (59)

ML-QEM Machine-learning quantum error mitigation Nature Machine Intelligence v. 6, p. 1478 (2024)

Machine learning accelerates error mitigation ML-QEM reduces the cost of quantum error mitigation without sacrificing accuracy. Pros: Arguably lowest runtime overhead, applies to multiple and generic expectation value, accelerates essentially any existing physics-based method … Cons: Could have biased expectation values, requires circuit-class specific training Practical utility metrics • Performance / precision • Cost / efficiency • Scalability • Applicability Disclaimer: No DeepSeek, ChatGPT, or Transformer moment here. First proof of concept with very simple ideas. Not be confused with the step of “learning device noise” in quasi-probability-based QEM approaches, e.g., PEC or Z. Why could ML-QEM be working? Physics based methods ML-QEM Skip learning quantum noise Complex general object; We care about the relationship of classical objects. Instead, show similar circuits. Learn classical output-only relationships Learn non-linear relationship b/w <O_noisy> and <O_target> + circuit features directly. Generically hard, but here simple. Convergence of global noise Experiment: Empirically, noise effect is to damp same-weight Paulis by very similar amount in most circuits Theory: log(d) convergence for random circuits.* Tailor the noise We can tailor & simplify the noise (twirl, DD, etc.) * Dalzell, et al. Random quantum circuits transform local noise into global white noise, Commun. Math. Phys. (2024). Z. Minev, IBM Quantum (53)

EXTRA

Some future directions 1. When trained with different noise parameters and their corresponding noisy expectation values, can we set all noise parameters encoded in GNN to the “good” values (i.e., set encoded gate error to 0, coherence times to infinity) to predict the ideal expectation values without ever training on ideal expectation values (and thus scalable)? 2. Can we instead regress the ideal and noisy expectation values of small-scale circuits onto the noise parameters to extract some noise parameters (e.g., avg. 2q gate error) of the backend, without running benchmarking experiments with additional quantum resources? 3. In ML-QEM, the training set can be optimized in terms of both size and type of the training circuits subject to design principles 4. ML-QEM can be more rigorously benchmarked against leading methods, such as PEC, PEA, and pulse-stretching ZNE arXiv: 2309.17368 Z. Minev, IBM Quantum (63)

Error mitigation and error correction Error mitigation: working with what you have • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost limitation suppress errors on classical results (expectation values) no extra qubits or hardware resources needed trades classical resources (post-processing) for lower error bad asymptotic scaling: high number of samples & circuits Error correction: protecting quantum information • • • • benefit q-cost c-cost challenge suppress & correct errors to arbitrarily small level very large qubit and hardware overhead decoding and encoding can be classically costly requires fault-tolerant operations and readout Zlatko Minev, IBM Quantum (67)

Classical hardness of chromatic polynomial χ(G, k) • Extremely well studied in complexity theory for 50+ years • Complexity of computing the chromatic polynomial is completely understood • #P-hard, #P-complete • Calculating P(G,k) exactly involves counting all possible valid colorings, a task that generally requires exponential time in the size of the graph for arbitrary G • Calculating the number of k=3 colorings of a graph χ(G,3) is the canonical example of a #P-complete problem • More generally, calculating the chromatic polynomial χ(G, k) is #P-hard (typically exponential or worse runtime) for all k (including negative integers and even all complex numbers) • Even planar graphs are #P-hard • No efficient classical approximation algorithms for computing χ(G, k) are known for any k, except for the three easy points k = 0, 1, 2 • And, no fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) exists for rational k>2 • BQP-complete (decision version): additive approximation of the chromatic polynomial on a planar graph can be achieved with a polynomial-time quantum algorithm Graphic: T. Key results 1. Using a general framework for ML for QEM approach, we enhance and survey a broad spectrum of simple to complex machine learning models (linear regression, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and graph neural network) 2. Random forest (RF) model consistently outperforms other models 3. On small-scale circuits, ML-QEM significantly and consistently outperforms digital ZNE with lower overhead over a diverse set of tasks, in both noisy classical simulations and hardware experiment 4. On large-scale circuits, we demonstrate in hardware experiment how ML-QEM can significantly improve efficiency of existing QEM methods, e.g., digital ZNE Haoran Liao, IBM Quantum (17)

What is Qiskit Metal? • A new open-source quantum-EDA tool from IBM • Written in python • Apache License 2.0 • IBM claims no ownership or rights to any device or code • If you add code to the Metal database, it is open and free for everyone to use, but are under no obligation to ever contribute code. • Major contributions get authorship credit for citations. • Follows a modular architecture • Qdesign is the primary instance for your circuit layout. • Qcomponents are the library of circuits, like “super” p-cells. • Renderers are the API interfaces between Metal and external software tools. • Analysis work with the returned data of renderers to determine quantum parameters. • Qgeometry is the internal database which allows your design to be generated natively in any external simulation software. What is deterministic/predictable and what is not? 1. The onset of an individual jump evolution is not predictable; although it is knowable from the null-event readout signal. 2. The individual jump evolution is deterministic (predictable if known to have started) for as long as it continues; it follows exactly the same path in every occurrence. 3. Whether an individual jump evolution completes (continues all the way to state |D>) is not predictable, which is why the passage quoted from our paper references the COMPLETED quantum jump. Although not predictable, noncompletion of a jump is knowable from the readout signal.

Tech Note T21: Estimating observables from sampled bit strings Note by Zlatko Minev, for John Watrous (2022-03) Background. An experiment on a quantum computer results in classical data. The exper0/1 iment samples nominally-identical copies of the same state ρ of the system some number of ⇢ n 0110... times M ∈ Z≥0 . For an n-qubit system, each of the M samples returns a single (classical) .. binary string, such as 0110 . . ., sampled from a distribution determined by ρ and the measure. ment basis. We call the empirical distribution of the M sampled bitstrings the counts, which is (repeated M times) a stochastic integer vector over the set of all 2n possible measurement outcomes, i.e., the binary strings of length n, denoted Σ = {00 . . . 00, 00 . . . 01, . . . , 11 . . . 11}. The classical counts data D Eis post-processed to compute some desired statistic, such as the expectation of some operator Ô ; e.g., some Pauli string ⟨ZIZI . . .⟩. <latexit Question. Given the sampling error, how close to true is our estimate of the derived statistic from the bitstrings? How does the sampling error in the bitstrings propagate through the computation? How many M shots should an experimentalist run to obtain a certain confidence? Measurement setup. Consider an n-qubit register over the binary alphabet Σ = {0, 1}⊗n = Zn2 , with the associated complex Euclidian space X . The register is characterized by a state ρ ∈ D (X ) [Watrous(2018), Sec. 2.1.2]. In general, for a measurement with possible outcomes a drawn from some alphabet Γ, each measurement outcome is associated with a measurement operator µ̂ (a) ∈ Pos (X ); i.e., using the mapping is µ : Γ → Pos (X ) [Watrous(2018), Eq. (2.199)]. The probability vector over the possible measurement outcomes is1 X p (a) = ⟨µ̂ (a) , ρ⟩ ∈ R , with 0 ≤ p (a) ≤ 1 and p (a) = 1 . T22: Bounding sum of operators Tech Note T22: Bounding sum of operators Zlatko K. Minev (2022-03) 22.1 Positive semidefinite operators Here, we prove Lemma 3.3 of Watrous (2018) in some detail and point out the neat technique used to cast a sum of operators as a product of operators in a larger, augmenting space, which mixes quantum states and amplitudes. All references in this section refer to Watrous (2018). Lemma 3.3 of Ref. Watrous (2018). Let X be a complex Euclidean space, let Σ be an alphabet, let u ∈ CΣ be a complex vector, and let {Pa : a ∈ Σ} ⊂ Pos (X ) be a collection of positive semidefinite operators. It holds that X X u (a) Pa ≤ ∥u∥∞ Pa (1) , a∈Σ a∈Σ where u (a) ∈ C denotes the a-th element of the vector u and the spectral operator norm is equally denoted ∥P ∥ = ∥P ∥∞ . In words, the spectral (infinity) norm of the sum of the operators weighted by the complex vector is bounded by the maximum (infinity) norm of u times the the spectral norm of the unweighted total sum. The largest absolute value of the elements of vector u is the ∞ -norm ∥u∥∞ = max (|u (0)|,|u (1)|,...). So, bound is set by the largest absolute value in the weights times the total norm of the unweighted sum. In a sense, this bounding value could represent a worst-case error. P a∈Σ Pa ≤ PFor a looser bound, we can use the triangle inequality property of the norm, ∥P ∥. a a∈Σ Proof. First, a few observations: 1. Pa = Pa† because Pa is positive semidefinite (see bottom of page 17). Recasting sum of operators as a matrix product. We would like to reframe the sum as an operator product equation to make use of the Schatten norm properties more directly. Tech Note T25: Are mixed states and random sampling of states equivalent? Random sampling of trajectories: mixed states, measurements, simulations, and convergence Note by Zlatko Minev. Abstract This work investigates the impact of noise channels and random sampling on quantum state measurements. We begin by considering an initial qubit state and analyze how a unitary noise channel affects the state. By employing a twirling procedure over a subset of Pauli operators, we generate two distinct measurement trajectories. We then compare the statistics of these trajectories with those obtained from a mixed state ensemble. Finally, we analyze the moments—including expectation and variance—of both the measurement outcomes and the probability estimates in a setting that mirrors a coin toss experiment. Our key result shows that, despite different constructions (regular mixed states versus trajectory sampling), the average measurement statistics remain equivalent, while their fluctuations capture the intrinsic shot noise. 1 of 11 T25: Are mixed states and random sampling of states equivalent? Zlatko Minev

Tech Note T26: Introduction to Many-Body Physics: Exploring Spin Models for Quantum Computing Scientists Zlatko K. Minev (2023-05) In this pedagogic note, we will introduce the fascinating realm of many-body physics to quantum information scientists through the exploration of spin models. Our focus will be on providing a beginner-friendly approach to understanding the concepts of Hamiltonians, energy levels, one-particle density matrices (OPDMs), and the effects of disorder. Think of this as a "Hello World" guide to gain an intuitive grasp of spin models, building upon the non-interacting Anderson model and primarily focusing on one-particle, one-dimensional problems. Whether you are a student or an enthusiast, we invite you to dive into the world of spins. 26 Introduction to Many-Body Physics: Exploring Spin Models for Quantum Computing Scientists 1 26.1 Anderson model . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 1 26.2 Anderson model with spins (hard-core bosons) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 2 26.3 Example integrals of motion in a toy model . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 10 I will assume you are familiar with qubits, spin, and some basic terms of many body systems. For background, see our lectures at the Qiskit Global Summer School, which are on the qiskit.org website and also on youtube.com. Spin models in many-body physics. Spin models play a crucial role in many-body physics. We use them to understand complex, collective behaviors of interacting particles, to devise simplified yet powerful frameworks to investigate fundamental physical principles, and to predict and design material properties. By helping us uncover insights and develop practical applications, spin models help drive scientific progress and guide technological advancements. So, let’s get familiar with them. 26.1 Anderson model In the Anderson model, particles (such as electrons) are assumed to hop between lattice sites in a regular lattice. For simplicity, let’s work with a spin model. Imagine a one-dimensional lattice of 6 sites as depicted in Fig. 1. Each site has a spin that can have a bosonic spin excitation or no excitation on it. Since we are working with spins at each site, we can have either zero or one excitations per site. The lattice can either have open or closed (i.e. periodic) boundary conditions. (b) (a) 0 1 2 3 4 1 5 2 0 3 5 4 Figure 1: One-dimensional (1D) Anderson spin model. The illustration portrays a one-dimensional spin chain with both open (top) and closed (bottom; meaning, periodic) boundary conditions forL = 6 spins. Each site is affected by a specific potential, defined by the on-site energy wi at site i. In this model, the interaction coupling ti,i+1 is presumed to involve only the nearest neighbors. We can at first assume translational invariance for all coefficients, wi = w and ti,i+1 = t. The hopping or tunneling rate is t and w is the on-site energy. Notice that the problem is translationally invariant the the periodic boundary conditions. Otherwise, it is almost translationally invariant except for the edges. How can we think of the origin of this Hamiltonian? How can we depict this system visually? Here is one way to think about it visually: t t t t t w w w w w w 0 1 2 3 4 5 We have illustrated a spin chain system with open boundary conditions here. The red arrows indicate the nearest neighbor hopping, controlled by the parameter t. The on-site energies, represented by blue marks below, are uniform and dictated by the parameter w. A useful perspective for understanding both the hopping term and the on-site energy is to envision particles moving within a specific potential energy landscape, for instance, the periodic sine wave depicted here. Disorder in the potential could introduce disorder in the potential energy at each site wi (and perhaps the hopping terms as well). How do we begin to understand the properties and dynamics of the system? For smaller system sizes, we can undertake a numerical diagonalization to examine the model. To simplify the process, let’s begin with distinct hard-core bosons — essentially, just spins. In this approach, we avoid the complexities of symmetrizing particles for indistinguishable bosons or fermions, making the ’c’ operators easier to handle directly, akin to how we interact with qubits.1 26.2 Anderson model with spins (hard-core bosons) Consider particle which are distinguishable spin-1/2 bosons. In terms of qubit Pauli operator on each site i, the single particle operators are 1 (2) ci = (Xi + iYi ) = |0⟩ ⟨1|i , 2 where the index i labels the spatial index of the spins. Keep in mind Xi is an operator in a 2L dimensional Hilbert space. Otherwise, these are the standard qubit Pauli operators.2 The on-site energy term is a scaled Pauli Z operator, 1 |0⟩ c†i ci = (I − Z) = |1⟩ ⟨1|i = |1⟩ 2   1 1 −1 1 . c†i ci − I = − Z = 1 2 2 2 ⟨0| ⟨1| 0 , and 1   For a brief moment, let’s call this last term Ŵi := w c†i ci − 12 I . Thus, the zero state |0⟩i has a lower energy expectation value with respect to this Hamiltonian term. In particular, Ŵi |0⟩i = − 12 w |0⟩i and Ŵi |1⟩i = + 12 w |1⟩i . These are eigenvectors and eigenvalues. If we assume, w > 0 and t = 0, then the ground state is |0⟩.3 The one particle (defined in the spin spatial basis) occupation or density corresponds to the operator ni := c†i ci . Notational convention: Sometimes, you will see ci = 12 (Xi − iYi ) = |1⟩ ⟨0|i in which case the ground state is though of as the |1⟩ state. Then, c†i ci = 12 (I − Z) = |0⟩ ⟨0|i and c†i ci − 21 I = 12 Z. 3 By the way, here we have been loose in our discussion, since we only looked at the single particle (trace out the rest of the system if you want or make L = 1). The interaction term is proportional to ⟨00| ⟨01| ⟨10| ⟨11|   |00⟩ 0  |01⟩ 1  , c†i ci+1 + c†i+1 ci = Xi Xi+1 + Yi Yi+1 =   |10⟩ 1 |11⟩ 0 which can be seen to be single particle number conserving since it does not change the parity of the two-qubit reduced blocks. The number of up and down spins in the blocks stay fixed. 26.2.1 Simple regime 1: Hopping-free, translationally-invariant, periodic-BC regime 26.2.1.1 Hamiltonian, eigenvalues (spectrum), and eigenvectors Let’s first get comfortable with the pictures we will use to analyze the more complex system by starting with the simplest one first that we can analyze analytically (since it’s nearly trivial) and we can easily plot numerically for small system sizes. Hence, consider the Hamiltonian of Eq. (1) with t = 0, H=w L−1 X  1 c†i ci − Iˆ 2 i=0 = −w L−1 X Zi . i=0 It’s easy to see what the eigenvectors, eigenvalues, and conserved quantities and quasi-particles are, since there are no interactions in the system. In other words, it’s not really a many body system as much as a collection of a bunch of single systems, a perfect place to start. Let’s check the basis state |b⟩ = |bL−1 · · · b1 b0 ⟩ with the L-bit binary string b; i.e., b ∈ ZL 2 , with bi ∈ {0, 1} for i = 0, . . . , L − 1. Because of the translational invariance of H, it doesn’t matter spin is up (or which site the single particle is on). Tech Note T27: Simple noise models Zlatko K. Minev (2023-08) In this little pedagogic guide, I review a few simple but key noise models. In particular, I focus on global depolarizing and bit-flip processes. I’ll sketch out various ways to see them and connect the dots to key concepts like average gate fidelity, entanglement fidelity. Plus, we’ll see how they fit with that fancy sparsePauli-Lindblad noise model, which which we use in tricks like probabilistic error cancelation (PEC) and twirled readout error mitigation (T-REX). Let’s explore! 27 Simple noise models 1 27.1 Depolarizing noise . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 1 27.1.1 Single qubit . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 1 27.1.2 n-qubit depolarizing channel . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4 27.2 Bit flip noise channel . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 6 27.2.1 Single qubit . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 6 27.3 Gate fidelity . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 7 27.3.1 State fidelity . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 7 27.3.2 Average gate fidelity and entanglement fidelity . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 7 27.4 Fidelity between a cNOT and a (Z,X) random process . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 9 27.5 Pauli conjugated by Pauli [MOVE] . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 10 27.5.1 Conjugation of target Pauli by ctrl-Pauli . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 11 27.1 Depolarizing noise This is Mother Nature’s sneaky way of saying, “I’m going to randomly destroy your system a little bit.” Specifically, with a certain probability p, she decides to completely erase all information in the system.
